turn_text: Good morning from WKYT News. I'm Bill Bryant and we welcome you to Kentucky Newsmakers. One of them in the past, you know, we were dependent upon in Kentucky on tobacco. and the federal price support system that propped up that industry for a long, long time. So a lot of my colleagues want to know why I want and where for about that connection. But obviously being in the majority is a lot more fun than being in the minority. So that allowed me, as a minority, when we were in the minority, allowed me to be able to get things done that on any other committee would have been probably impossible. But because of the collegial nature of that committee, which I later chaired when we were in the majority, allows us as members of that committee to do things that we otherwise couldn't do. And I've been to the emergency rooms and to funerals and the like of kids, young people especially, victim of this insidious addiction. The heads of all of these organizations at that summit And they began to learn about what U.K. was capable of doing. In fact, I'm going to visit with Dr. Capilouto in a few minutes to talk about it, but it's going great. Your thoughts as miners block a shipment of coal from leaving in southeast Kentucky, the black jewel of coal mine that his declared bankruptcy, those folks worked, their paychecks bounced, as you know. When it happened, and it became involved in the bankruptcy legal proceedings, it sort of limited what some of us could try to do, because it's a court thing. But this issue is going to be going on for a while. There's so many different ramifications of it. I'm not on the committee that deals with that in a direct sense, although Brett Guthrie from Bowling Green is. So we'll see how it goes. You pay much attention to in-state politics? You're watching the governor's race? Absolutely. Yeah. How do you see that right now? Well, I'm for Governor Bevin. Strong. I think he's doing good. I think he's coming on really well. It is also, as you know, co-chair with me of the SOAR initiative, a shaping our Appalachian region based in Pineville to try to reshape the economy of East Kentucky and to remodel it. Those flood walls we built early in the 80s, Those towns don't flood anymore. And that, to me, is great stuff. Congressman, thanks for coming. We appreciate it. Thank you.
